versions: You come down out of the hills into the Marches at dusk, a letter of passage in your coat and a long way still to go. A woman waits by a boat at the foot of the road, watching you come.
> You show the ferrywoman the long scar on my left cheek and ask if she remembers me.

Her eyes go wide with recognition, then narrow as she studies your face more closely. She's older than you remember - sun-darkened skin lined with years of hard work, gray strands mixed through her dark hair. Her gaze settles on the scar and stays there.

"You're that bastard who killed three guards at the river crossing," she says, her voice flat and bitter. "The one they told me was hanged." She spits into the water. "That letter won't do you any good now."

Behind her, a man emerges from the ferry house with a crossbow in his hands. The weapon isn't aimed at you yet, but he's got you covered.
> You unwrap my grandfather's bronze sword, Dawnsplitter, and set it on the table.

The ferryman's crossbow snaps up, his finger finding the trigger. The ferrywoman slams her palm down on the table, sending your letter skittering to the ground.

"Bronze?" she laughs, a harsh sound like breaking glass. "You think that scrap of copper makes you anything but a fool, boy?" She kicks over a bucket of salt water, drenching both the sword and your boots. "That river's deeper than your grandfather's grave."

The ferryman doesn't lower his weapon. Behind him, shadows move in the ferry house - other passengers waiting to cross, or hired muscle keeping them there.
> You favour my right knee as I walk; it was broken last winter and never set straight.

The ferrywoman notices the limp immediately, her eyes following the hitch in your stride like a predator tracking wounded prey. "That's why you're here," she says, pointing with a gnarled finger. "Can't farm with a bad leg, can't fight with a crippled knee. You think this passage will buy you an easier life."

She gestures to the ferryman without breaking eye contact. The crossbow swings toward you as he advances, his boots crunching on wet gravel. Salt from the bucket stings your scraped palms where the sword landed.

"Easier lives cost more than pieces of paper," she continues, her words hushed and menacing. "The Baron pays well for river crossers who don't reach the other side."
> You say "My name is Oriel Vance. I am a cartographer out of Hallow Down."

The ferrywoman's face shifts, her lined features arranging themselves into something almost resembling interest. She doesn't relax, but she doesn't reach for the cleaver at her belt either.

"Vance," she repeats slowly, testing the name like wine for poison. "I knew a cartographer named Vance years back. Drowned himself mapping the rapids upstream." Her gaze flicks to the water behind her. "You carrying any of his work?"

The ferryman keeps his crossbow trained on you, though he's moved close enough now that you can smell the fish scales and lamp oil on him. Behind him in the ferry house, someone clears their throat - a reminder that there are ears listening to every word.
> You say "Is anyone there?"

"Is that supposed to be clever?" The ferrywoman barks out a laugh, though her eyes remain cold and sharp. "Course there's someone there - that's why you ain't dead yet." She jerks her thumb toward the ferry house without turning around.

From the shadows inside emerges a tall woman in the gray-green robes of a healer. Her hands are stained with blood, but she moves with the smooth confidence of someone who has killed before and knows how to do it cleanly.

"Cartographers don't usually travel alone this time of year," the ferrywoman says, her voice dropping lower. "Especially not ones with bounties on their heads." She scoops up your letter from where it fell and waves it at you. "This here's good for one crossing, but that don't buy safety."
> You note that the ferry landing sits on the north bank, below the broken mill.

The ferrywoman follows your gaze to the crumbling mill wheel above them, its wooden slats warped by years of seasonal floods. "Aye, smart lad," she says, though her tone remains hostile. "That's the north bank - and this here's the last ferry point before you hit the Baron's territory."

She gestures toward the southern shore where torches flicker in the growing dusk. The lights seem deliberately placed to catch any movement in the water, like teeth in a trap.

"Baron keeps a dozen crossbow men on that side," she continues, watching your face for any reaction. "They shoot anything that moves across without his blessing - even if it's just a piece of driftwood."
> You find the trapdoor to the cellar behind the inn's kitchen hearth.

The trapdoor creaks open under your weight, releasing a stench of mold and decay that makes your eyes water. Stairs descend into absolute darkness, each wooden step slick with condensation and something else you don't want to identify. Halfway down, your boot catches on a loose board and sends it crashing into the cellar floor below.

Voices rise from the inn above - chairs scraping, feet moving quickly across floorboards. Someone shouts "Check the cellar!" in the healer's voice, but her words sound distorted by the damp air seeping up from below.

The basement stretches before you, just visible in the dim light filtering through a single barred window near the ceiling. Shelves line the walls, but their contents lie in shadow. In the center of the room stands an old wooden table with iron shackles bolted to its surface.
> You leave Tamsin at her ferry on the river and walk inland alone.

The ferrywoman spits into the river as you step onto the gravel bank. "Crossing alone don't make you brave, boy," she calls after you, her voice carrying easily over the water's murmur. "Just means there ain't nobody left to bury you."

You hike through a narrow gully lined with birch saplings that crackle underfoot like breaking bones. The path leads uphill past an abandoned sheepfold where wind whistles through the rotting walls, then levels out onto moorland dotted with standing stones worn smooth by centuries of rain.

Behind you, the ferry's horn sounds twice - the signal for departing passengers. But it seems wrong somehow, the timing off like a broken clock. You turn and see no boat on the water, just swirling currents where the current is strongest.
> You walk the earthen wall around the village to its single gate, the only way in.

The earthen wall rises to your chest, topped with broken glass embedded in clay. As you round the last corner, a wooden post bearing a human skull blocks the path - fresh bones still clinging to rotting sinew. Beyond it, the village's single gate stands open but no torches burn in the courtyard beyond.

A bell chimes once from somewhere inside, its sound swallowed by the mist that now hangs thick between you and the gate. The air smells of damp wool and something else - a sharp chemical bite that makes your eyes water and your nose burn.

Movement flickers in the darkness ahead: shapes too large to be shadows shifting between buildings. A voice calls out in the same healer's tone from earlier, though it's been altered somehow - higher pitched, almost feminine.
> You watch the clouds gather.

Dark clouds pile up over the village like a funeral shroud, their underbellies rippling with sickly green light that pulses in time to your heartbeat. The mist thickens, pressing against your skin like cold hands, and from the courtyard comes a sound that might be singing or screaming—you can't tell which.

Something wet strikes your shoulder—at first you think it's rain, but the droplets feel too warm and when you wipe at them, they smear red across your palm. The smell of copper intensifies as more droplets fall, painting the earthen wall in a crimson stripe that glows faintly in the unnatural light.
> You tug the patch over my missing left eye straight; a falconer's bird took the eye years ago.

The patch hangs crooked despite your efforts, its black leather damp from the unnatural mist that clings to everything around you. The red droplets continue falling, hissing where they hit the earthen wall and leaving scalded stone behind.

From the village comes a new sound - metal striking stone, regular as a heartbeat. Between the buildings, something pale moves with the rhythm of a pendulum swing. The green light pulses brighter, and in its glow you see the skull at your feet is still warm, flesh hanging in ribbons from its exposed jaw.

The mist thickens further, obscuring the gate entirely now. But the sound of metal against stone grows closer, and with it comes another noise - a wet dragging, as if something heavy is being pulled across cobblestones.
> You refuse to go near the horses; I have been afraid of them since one threw me as a child.

The horses whinny and stamp their hooves at your approach, sensing your fear as clearly as if it were smoke pouring from your skin. Their handler - a grizzled old man with rope burns scarring his hands - eyes you with the sharp attention of someone who's survived this trade through reading men's tells.

"You're the cartographer, then," he says, spitting tobacco juice into the dirt between his boots and the horses. "Heard you were coming. They said you'd be stupid enough to try riding with us." His laugh is a wet, hacking sound. "Guess they was right."
> You say "My sister Lenna keeps the lighthouse at Gull Point. I send her every coin I can spare."

The ferrywoman's face shifts, her lined features relaxing just enough to let you see the woman beneath the bitterness. "Gull Point," she repeats softly, as if testing the name for hidden meaning. "That's two weeks' hard riding from here - if you don't run into Baron Blackmore's men."

She glances back toward her ferry house where shadows still move in the doorway, then steps closer, lowering her voice. "Your sister's got a reputation there, boy. Word is she talks to the lights at night - channels them across the water like signals between ships."

The ferryman's crossbow wavers slightly as he leans forward to listen, his finger still hovering near the trigger. Behind him, the healer emerges fully from the shadows, her bloodstained hands now wrapped in cloth that does little to hide the fresh scratches across her knuckles.
> You roll up my sleeve to show the stranger the blue heron tattooed on my forearm.

The ferrywoman's eyes narrow as she studies the tattoo, her work-worn fingers brushing against your arm before you can pull away. "Blue heron," she mutters, spitting into the water again. "That's Caelin's mark - but he's been dead these three years."

The ferryman behind her shifts uneasily, his crossbow wavering as he watches this exchange. From the shadows of the ferry house comes a low whistle - a signal or a warning, it's impossible to tell which.

"Your grandda drew that on you?" The ferrywoman's voice carries new suspicion now, her rough fingers still pressing into your arm like she's checking for falsehood. "Because Caelin only did his own work, and he never marked any boy who wasn't blood or bound."
> You sleep until first light.

Dawn creeps over the moors like a fever dream, turning the mist into glistening threads of silver that cling to your clothes and hair. You wake shivering under a thin blanket of heather that offers little comfort from the night's chill.

The village below remains silent as a tomb, its gate still standing open like a mouth that never closes. Fresh blood stains mark the path where you walked - whether from some nocturnal predator or your own wounds, you cannot tell. Your left knee throbs in time to your pulse, the broken bone protesting against the hard ground.

The sun climbs higher, burning off the worst of the mist and revealing more of the village's layout. A well sits at its center surrounded by the blackened remains of what were once market stalls. The buildings themselves lean at impossible angles, their windows empty eye sockets staring down at the courtyard where something metallic still glints in the sunlight.
> You climb the bell tower on the hill; its bell is cracked and has not rung in years.

The bell tower's wooden steps groan under your weight as you climb, each board slick with decades of rainwater and worse fluids. At the top, the bell sways gently in a draft that carries something foul - charred meat mixed with rotting cloth.

Through the broken windows, the moors stretch gray and empty in every direction. But as your eyes adjust to the gloom, you see smoke rising from multiple points on the horizon - small fires burning in what should be farmland. The bell itself hangs at a strange angle, its clapper missing entirely, leaving only a gaping wound in the bronze.
> You cross the rope bridge over the gorge west of the village, testing each plank; three are missing.

The rope groans under your weight as you test the first plank with your boot, finding solid wood beneath the moss. The second board creaks ominously but holds. When you step onto the third, there's nothing - only empty air where a rotted plank once hung.

You lunge forward to grab the next intact board, but your bad knee buckles at the last moment. Your fingers scrabble at the rope, finding purchase just as your body swings over the gorge's edge. Wind rushes past as you dangle three hundred feet above jagged rocks that jut like broken teeth from a churning river below.
> You leave an offering at the shrine of the antlered god in the birch wood.

The birch trees stand white and silent as bones against the gray sky, their bark scarred with old bloodstains where previous offerings were made. At the clearing's center, an altar of black stone bears the crude carving of an antlered head, its eyesockets empty and hungry.

You unwrap the bread and salt from your pack - meager offerings for a god who demands sacrifice in blood. The wind picks up as you kneel before the altar, carrying with it whispers in languages that predate the Marches. Something wet drops onto your neck from above; when you reach to wipe it away, your fingers come back red.
> You visit the healer, old Brannoch, whose hut stands on stilts in the marsh east of the village.

Brannoch emerges from his hut as you approach, the wooden platform groaning under his massive frame. His beard hangs like seaweed, and his hands bear ritual scars that tell stories older than the Marches themselves.

"Another cartographer," he rumbles, his voice like stones grinding together. "The third this season to seek my aid. The others didn't make it to Gull Point - their bones fertilize the bog now." His yellowed eyes study your face with clinical interest. "You've got the look of a man who knows death is coming and wants to outrun it."
> You say "Fair weather for travelling."

Brannoch lets out a sound that might be laughter if it weren't so bone-deep. "Fair weather?" His massive hands gesture toward the gray sky where the twin moons peer through thinning clouds. "You'll be dead of fever before you reach the halfway point, cartographer."

He spits into the marsh water below, where something pale swirls beneath the surface. "The roads east are crawling with Baron Blackmore's tax collectors - they shoot first and ask questions after the blood's stopped flowing." His scarred fingers trace patterns in the air that seem to shimmer briefly before dissolving. "Course, that might be better than what's waiting for you west of here."
> You look around.

The marsh water laps against the hut's stilts, black and thick as blood. Wooden planks bridge the smaller channels, but the gaps between them reveal depths where pale shapes twist beneath the surface - too large to be fish but too small to be men.

Brannoch watches your eyes track the movement, his scarred hands folding into themselves like old parchment. "Those ain't the bog-wolves," he says, reading your thoughts with unsettling accuracy. "Just their young - still learning to swim in the deeper pools."

He spits again, this time watching the glob disappear into the murk. "Baron's got new ways of collecting debts. Sends his men out with nets and iron hooks to drag people back from the water. Course, most of them don't make it that far - the deeper bogs keep what they take."
> You follow the path east.

The path toward the eastern moors leads through a landscape that seems deliberately designed to kill anyone foolish enough to tread it. Patches of quicksand masquerade as solid ground, their surfaces deceptively firm until you step onto them and feel the world sink away beneath your feet. Brannoch's hut shrinks to a black speck behind you as the path narrows between stands of twisted thornbushes whose branches end in wicked barbs.

Ahead, the trail splits - one fork leads directly east toward higher ground where smoke from distant chimneys promises shelter and warmth. The other winds north through a grove of dead trees whose skeletal branches creak like breaking bones in the wind. From that direction comes a rhythmic pounding that might be hammers on anvil or something far more sinister.
> You listen for anything moving.

The wind through the thornbushes sounds like fingernails on slate, and somewhere beyond the path, water sloshes against something solid. A single drop of moisture - rain or something else - strikes the back of your neck, and when you reach to wipe it off, your fingers come away sticky and warm.

The rhythmic pounding from the north grows louder now, punctuated by what sounds like a human voice screaming between hammer blows. The eastern path remains clear, though wisps of mist rise from pools in the road that weren't there moments ago. Behind you, the path to Brannoch's hut has already begun to disappear under creeping bog water that flows with purpose.
> You say "Is anyone there?"

Brannoch spits into the murky water below his hut, where pale shapes continue their lazy swimming. His scarred fingers drum against the wooden railing as he considers your question with the patience of a man who's outlived better thinkers.

"Course there's someone there," he rumbles finally, his voice grinding like millstones. "That's why you ain't dead yet." His massive head tilts toward the shadows inside his hut where something moves in the darkness—too large to be a shadow and too silent to be breathing. "Baron's got his men out with nets tonight, looking for runaways to drag back east."
> You check my pack.

Your pack feels lighter than it should - something has shifted inside during the climb. When you open it, half your rations are gone, replaced by a handful of iron nails wrapped in bloodstained cloth. The smell hits you immediately - not just rust, but something else, something organic that makes your stomach clench.

Brannoch's yellowed eyes track your movements as you pull out the cloth. "Baron's men get cleverer every season," he rumbles with grim satisfaction. "Leave their mark in places that don't show when you're searched at the crossing."

The iron nails feel warm in your palm, almost fever-hot against your skin. As you examine them more closely, you notice each one bears tiny scratches - not from being hammered, but as if something has been clawing at them in its death throes.
> You rest a while in the shade.

The thornbushes provide scant shelter as you settle against their twisted trunks, but their shadow is marginally cooler than the open moorland. As you close your eyes, the rhythmic pounding from the northern path grows closer—metal striking bone rather than anvil now, accompanied by wet, tearing sounds that speak of butchery rather than craft.

Brannoch's hut creaks behind you as the tide shifts in the marsh below, and something large splashes into deeper water. The iron nails in your pack feel heavier now, pressing against your ribs like a cancer spreading through bone. When you open your eyes, you see fresh scratches in the mud beside your feet—finger-length gouges that weren't there when you sat down.
> You drink from my waterskin.

The water tastes of copper and something else—something foul that makes your tongue burn and throat constrict. Halfway through drinking, you realize the liquid isn't actually water at all, but some kind of tainted distillation that's already affecting your vision. The world tilts slightly as your body begins shutting down systems it can no longer trust.

Brannoch's massive form looms closer, his yellowed eyes bright with satisfaction. "Poison from the deep bogs," he rumbles as you stumble toward the hut's edge. "Been saving it for someone special."

The marsh water below churns with pale shapes that weren't there before—bodies dissolving in the acidic muck, their bones already stripped clean by things that hunt in the depths. Your legs give out completely as the poison reaches your brain, and you find yourself falling toward the black water where something waits with open maws.

The mist thickens, pressing against your skin like cold hands, and from the village below comes a sound that might be singing or screaming—you can't tell which.

Something wet strikes your shoulder—at first you think it's rain, but the droplets feel too warm and when you wipe at them, they smear red across your palm. The smell of copper intensifies as more droplets fall, painting the earthen wall in a crimson stripe that glows faintly in the unnatural light.
> You walk on until dusk.

The eastern path stretches ahead like a wound across the moorland, marked by scattered stones that seem to whisper warnings in languages older than the Marches themselves. Each step sends fresh waves of poison through your system, making the world lurch and sway around you. The tainted water in your gut burns like acid, but stopping now would mean certain death from exposure.

Ahead, smoke rises from a cluster of huts built into a rocky outcrop - the first sign of civilization since you left Brannoch's marsh behind. But as you draw closer, you see the structures are empty shells, their doors hanging open on broken hinges and their interiors dark with ash. Whatever happened here was violent and recent.
> You say "A long road for a short errand."

Brannoch spits into the black water below, watching the glob dissolve among the pale shapes swimming in the murk. "Long roads make short men," he rumbles, his scarred hands gripping the hut's railing as if preparing to throw you over. "But that don't matter much to Baron Blackmore's tax collectors."

The wind picks up, carrying with it the distant echo of hammering from the northern path. Brannoch's yellowed eyes follow your gaze toward the sound, his massive head nodding slowly. "They've been at it all day - breaking bones and making sure the screams carry far enough to keep other fools from coming this way."
> You make camp and light a small fire.

The fire smolders weakly in the circle of stones you've gathered, its smoke thin and gray in the heavy air. Brannoch watches from his hut as you huddle closer to the flames, his massive frame silhouetted against the black water below.

"Foolish boy," his voice carries across the marsh like a funeral dirge. "You think that little spark will keep the bog-wolves away? They can smell warm blood from a league off, and yours is calling them even now."

The poison continues eating through your system, each pulse of pain bringing fresh waves of nausea. The firelight reveals more details of the abandoned huts ahead - splintered door frames and walls blackened by fire that was set with careful aim, suggesting whoever lived here was given time to watch their homes burn.
> You sleep until first light.

Dawn crawls over the moors like a wound opening, painting everything in shades of gray that make your eyes water and your head throb. The fire has died to embers, leaving only ash and the acrid taste of failure in your mouth. Your waterskin hangs empty, its leather skin hardened by the tainted liquid that nearly killed you.

Brannoch's hut groans as he stirs within, his massive frame causing the stilts to creak like bones breaking. The black water below churns with fresh movement - pale shapes cutting through the murk with deadly purpose. Your left knee screams in protest as you stand, the broken bone grinding against itself whenever you move.
> You wash my face in the stream.

Cold water splashes against your skin, washing away the grime and salt from the ferry crossing. The stream runs swift here, cutting through a narrow ravine that echoes with the rush of water over stone. As you cup your hands for another drink, something dark floats past - a severed finger, its bone white and flesh green with decay.

Brannoch watches from his stilted hut as you dry your face, his yellow eyes tracking every movement. "Clean skin don't mean clean soul in these parts," he rumbles across the marsh. "That water's been tainted by everything that's ever died upstream - including the ferrywoman's crew."
> You count the coins I have left.

You spread your remaining coins across a flat stone beside the stream - five silver pennies, a bent copper bar, and two iron nails that weren't in your pack before. The ferrywoman's poison has made your thoughts sluggish, but even through the haze you realize something is wrong. Those iron nails shouldn't be there, and the copper bar looks too clean to have survived your journey this far.

Brannoch calls out from his hut across the marsh: "Counting coins don't change what they're worth here, cartographer. Baron's men mark everything they touch with their stink - makes it worthless to anyone who matters."
> You ask a passing carter for news.

The carter spits tobacco juice into the stream before answering, his lined face grim beneath a cap stained with sweat and mud. "News?" he barks out a laugh that turns into a wet cough. "News is the Baron's got new ways of collecting taxes - starts with your fingers and works inward from there."

His wagon creaks as he shifts his weight, revealing a stump where his left hand once was. Fresh bandages wrapped around the wound smell of rot and old blood. "Ferrywoman at Tamsin's Crossing? She ain't been seen since yesterday - neither has her crew or the passengers who tried to cross after you."

> You climb the low ridge ahead.

The ridge's top crumbles under your boots, sending loose stones clattering down its face to splash in the stream below. From this vantage point, the moors stretch gray and empty in every direction—no smoke rises from any chimney, no movement stirs the thornbushes, and even the pale shapes in Brannoch's bog have gone still.

But ahead, past where the stream cuts through a narrow canyon of black rock, you see something that makes your heart stop. A column of smoke rises from what should be empty wasteland, too thick and black to be from a cooking fire. As you watch, figures move between the distant rocks—too far to make out details, but their numbers suggest this isn't some isolated camp.
> You wait for the rain to pass.

The rain slants sideways across the moors, turning the path into a slick of mud and pebbles that makes each step treacherous. Brannoch hunches lower in his hut as the storm intensifies, his massive shoulders hunched against the wind that howls through the marsh below.

After what feels like hours but is likely less than one, the downpour eases to a steady drizzle. You step from beneath the thornbush where you've taken shelter and feel your boots immediately sink ankle-deep in the newly saturated earth. The path ahead has been transformed into a maze of rivulets and standing pools that could hide all manner of hazards beneath their deceptively calm surfaces.
> You sharpen my blade.

The whetstone grinds against your blade's edge with a steady rasp that drowns out the sounds of Brannoch stirring in his hut above. The metal grows warm under your hands as you work, each pass removing tiny layers to reveal the steel beneath the rust and neglect.

Brannoch leans heavily against his hut's railing, watching you through yellowed eyes. "That blade won't help you when they come for it," he rumbles, his voice carrying across the marsh like stones grinding together. "Baron's men take steel from corpses and living folk alike - their collection grows every season."
> You press on towards the village.

The path narrows as you approach the village, thornbushes closing in on both sides like hungry mouths. Ahead, the blackened remains of a market stall lean against the well at impossible angles, their charred posts pointing toward the gray sky like accusing fingers.

From the courtyard beyond comes a rhythmic scraping sound—metal dragged across stone. Between the buildings, something pale and too large to be human moves in a pendulum swing, its motion accompanied by wet dragging. The air carries an oppressive stillness, broken only by the drip of moisture from your clothes and the distant echo of hammering from the northern path.

The village center reveals itself as you round the final bend—twisted posts lean at impossible angles like broken ribs, and a well sits at the courtyard's heart, its bucket dangling empty above black water that reflects nothing. The whetstone grinds against your blade's edge with a steady rasp that drowns out the distant sounds from beyond the thornbush. The metal grows warm under your hands as you work, each stroke removing tiny flakes of rust and steel until the edge gleams dully in the dying light.

Brannoch watches you through yellowed eyes as you pull out the cloth wrapping. "Baron's men get clever each season," he rumbles with satisfaction, never pausing his work with the clay jar. "Leave their mark where it won't be found during a search." The iron nails feel fever-hot in your palms as you examine them closer, deep scratches visible—claw marks from something that tried to escape its fate.
> You press on towards the village.

Thornbush tears at your sleeves as you force your way through the bone grove toward Tamsin, whose dark hair is now completely matted with dried blood. The village reeks of rotting meat and something sweet underneath that turns your stomach—sugar and death. Tamsin lies collapsed beside her grisly skull arrangement, dark hair now frozen in congealed gore, her breath coming in shallow gasps that fog the chilled air.

Brannoch grinds his herbs in the distance, spitting occasionally into the dark water below as he mutters about the poor dead woman. The wet sounds from deeper in village have stopped entirely—leaving only the wind whistling through collapsed buildings and your own labored breathing in the cold air.
